texts.preamble: Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1.
texts.facts: 1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules. The accused no.1 is stated to be the vendor cum proprietor of M/s. Diamond Bakers, from where the Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1. Ashok Kumar on 22 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144496466/ 1 food article, that is, 'Sugar Boiled Confectionery' was lifted for sampling. Accused no.2 is stated to be the proprietor of M/s. Sanjay Traders from whom the vendor had purchased the food article. Accused no.5 Company is stated to be the manufacturer / supplier from whom the supplier / accused no.2 had purchased the food article, of which accused no.3 (since discharged) was the Nominee for Sales Depot and accused no.4 was the Nominee for manufacturing unit. 2. As per the complaint, on 22.11.2005, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) A. K. Singh and Field Assistant (FA) Ashok Kumar under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. S. B. Kaloria reached along with their staff at the premises of accused no.1 at Shop No. 2, Sector - 4, R. K. Puram, New Delhi-22, where the accused no.1 was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption. The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of 'Sugar Boiled Confectionery' from the vendor that was lying in sealed packets of 515 gram each bearing identical label declaration, to which he agreed. A sample of three such sealed packets was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules. Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama etc. The price of sample was paid to the vendor. Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA. Vide report dated 22.12.2005, the PA found the sample to be misbranded on the ground that it gave misleading declaration regarding the presence of some colors. Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI. It was found that accused no.2 had supplied the food article to accused no.1 vendor and further that the food article had been manufactured by accused no.5 company, of which accused no.3 (since expired) was the nominee of the sales depot and accused no.4 was the nominee at the manufacturing unit. After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA. The complaint was then filed in the court on 22.12.2006 alleging violation of section 2(ix)(g) and (k) of PFA Act, read with rule 37 of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act. 3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned. The accused appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL). The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL. The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 17.02.2007, opining the sample to be not conforming to the standards on the ground that it contained permitted synthetic colors more than the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm. 4. In the meanwhile, on an application moved under section 294 CrPC, vide order dated 27.10.2009, the accused no.1 to 2 were given the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of PFA Act on the basis of an admitted invoice and they were discharged. Accused no.3 also expired during the proceedings of the case and the proceedings against him stood abated vide order dated 20.10.2008. Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1. Ashok Kumar on 22 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144496466/ 2 5. Based on the CFL report, pre charge evidence was led wherein PW1 FI A. K. Singh was examined by the prosecution. Based on his testimony, charge was framed against accused no.4 and 5 on 18.02.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of PFA Act read with Rule 30 of PFA Rules, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 6. At the trial, prosecution examined three witness in support of its case. PW-1 FI A. K. Singh, PW-2 Sh. S. P. Kaloria and PW-3 FA Ashok Kumar were a part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings. They deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 22.11.2005 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 3 sealed packets of 515 gram each of 'Sugar Boiled Confectionery', separately sealing, marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses. They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, notice Ex. PW-1/B, panchnama Ex. PW-1/C, notice under section 14A Ex. PW1/D, raid report Ex. PW-2/A, PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/E and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/F. PA report Ex. PW-1/G was received and investigation was started. Letters Ex. PW-1/H to Ex. PW1/N pertain to the correspondence between the FI, the accused persons and the government agencies to ascertain their constitution and role during the course of investigation. After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/O was taken from the Director PFA. The complaint Ex. PW-1/P was filed in the court. A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/Q was sent to the accused persons vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/R. These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that representative sample was not taken or that the label declaration was not identical on all the packets or that the accused persons had been falsely implicated. 7. Statements of the accused no.4 and accused no.5 (through AR) under section 313 CrPC were recorded on 30.04.2013 wherein they denied the knowledge about the sample proceedings but claimed that the reports of analysts were not reliable being at variation. They chose to lead evidence in defence. 8. Accused no.4 examined himself as DW-1 as the only defence witness. He informed that he was nominee of the manufacturing unit of the company in 1996 but vide subsequent resolution dated 29.04.2000 Ex. DW-1/A, his previous nomination stood superseded. He stated that the nominee for Delhi region was Mr. S. C. Sawhney who not be implicated due to his death.
texts.arguments: 9. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against both the accused no.4 and 5 beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused persons have not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 17.02.2007 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive. It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no contradiction can be seen in their testimony. 10. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various missing links in the testimony of the witnesses. Ld. Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1. Ashok Kumar on 22 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144496466/ 3 Counsel has strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore, conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report. He has relied upon the various judgements in his support. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a) it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned. 15. In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents. For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director.... It means obliterate, [LEAKAGE_MASK], annul, replace, make void, inefficacious or useless, repeal. It will be anomalous to hold that for some purpose it survives and for other purposes it is superseded." However, the defence strongly relies upon the judgement titled as Kanshi Nath v. State [2005(2) FAC 219], informing that Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1. Ashok Kumar on 22 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144496466/ 4 the said ruling has been constantly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in State v. Ramesh Chand [2010 (2) JCC 1250], Food Inspector v. Parvinder Malik [2014(2) FAC 306], State v. Vinod Kumar Gupta [2010(2) JCC 957], State v. Virender Kohli [2014(2) FAC 223], State v. Kamal Aggarwal [2014(2) FAC 183], State v. Vidya Gupta [2014(1) FAC 291], State v. Dinesh Goswami [2014(1) FAC 302], State v. Mahabir [2014(1) FAC 286], State v. Santosh Sharma [2014(1) FAC 296], Raja Ram Seth & Sons v. Delhi Administration [2012(2) FAC 523], State v. Sunil Dutt [2011(4) JCC 2377] and State v. Rama Rattan Malhotra [2012(2) FAC 398]. It is submitted that comparison of the two reports would show that there are substantive variations which would show that the sample was not representative. 17. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Kashi Nath's case (supra), was dealing with a situation where there were certain variations in the reports of PA and CFL while analysing a sample of 'dhania powder'. Hon'ble Court considered the ratio in MCD v. Bishan Sarup [ILR 1970 (1) Delhi 518] and held that it would still be open for the accused to establish that the sample tested was not a representative one, and if the variation in the two reports is substantial enough, then the PA report can certainly be looked into to establish this variation. 18.
